sections.heading: What We Look For First
body: Most plumbing calls come down to one worn part, a clog or a bad seal. Here is what we check before anyone talks about replacing anything.

items.title: A water heater that's gone cold
items.text: A thermostat, a heating element or a gas valve can be the whole problem, and any of them is a smaller job than a new tank. If the tank itself has failed, you'll hear that too.

items.title: A drain that's slow or backing up
items.text: A clog is a clearing job, not a replacement job. We clear it, then look at why it formed, whether that's grease, roots or a pipe that's failing.

items.title: A leak under a sink or in a wall
items.text: Often a worn seal, a bad valve or a cracked fitting. We find the real source before anyone opens a wall.

items.title: A faucet or tub that won't stop dripping
items.text: Cheap parts and tired seals cause a lot of these. Rebuilding is sometimes an option before replacing the whole fixture.

items.title: A sewer line that keeps backing up
items.text: A backup doesn't always mean a new line. We look for where it's blocked or broken first, and when the pipe has really failed, we say so.

items.title: A water line that's broken or leaking
items.text: A break between the city main and the house gets found, explained, and then repaired or replaced.

sections.heading: What Happens When You Call About Your Water Heater

image.alt: Front door of a Wichita home, where the visit starts

body: Tell us what the heater is doing: no hot water, not enough of it, a puddle, a noise. We'll tell you what we think it is.
Then we look at the heater and find what actually failed. If it's a small part or a setting, we fix that. If it's the tank, you'll hear that too, with your options.
A cold shower on a Saturday is a normal call for us. We work seven days a week and don't charge emergency rates.

sections.heading: What Usually Goes Wrong
body: A water heater is a tank, a heat source, a thermostat and a few valves. When one piece fails, the whole thing feels dead, even when the rest of it is fine.
Here's what we check first.

items.title: No hot water at all
items.text: On a gas heater, the pilot or the gas valve. On an electric one, a tripped breaker, a failed element or a bad thermostat. These are small parts, and fixing one is a smaller job than a new heater.

items.title: Hot water that runs out fast
items.text: A failed element or a thermostat set too low can cut the supply. So can sediment built up in the bottom of the tank. We check these before anyone suggests a bigger heater.

items.title: Water that's only lukewarm
items.text: Often the thermostat setting or a worn element. It's worth ruling those out before anything else.

items.title: A puddle around the tank
items.text: Water at a fitting or a valve can be repaired. Water coming from the body of the tank means the tank has failed, and no repair will hold. We'll tell you which one you have.

items.title: Rumbling or popping from the tank
items.text: Usually sediment cooking at the bottom. It's a warning, not an emergency, and worth a look before it turns into a leak.

items.title: Rusty or discolored hot water
items.text: This can point to a tank corroding from the inside. If the cold water runs clear and only the hot is rusty, the heater is the place to look.

sections.quote: Called Brandon this afternoon to come look at our hot water heater that was leaking. … he was so kind and actually replaced our hot water heater. Hes very knowledgeable and reasonably priced.

sections.heading: Repair or Replace?

image.alt: Hand turning on a bathroom faucet with steam rising

body: Here's a rule you can check. If it's a thermostat, an element, a valve or a fitting, repair it. That's a smaller job than a new heater, and the heater goes on working.
If the tank is leaking from its body, the heater is old and the repairs are stacking up, or the same part keeps failing, price a new one. Money spent on a tank that's finished doesn't come back.
We lay the two side by side and tell you which side you're on, including when the answer is repair.

sections.quote: Brandon was super responsive and honest about the pros and cons compared to a tank system. He ended up quoting quite a bit less than some of the others I called and got it installed quickly.
sections.name: Marcee L.

sections.heading: When You Do Need a New One
body: When the tank is done, we replace it. We'll walk through your choices, including the downsides of each, so you pick the heater and nobody picks it for you.
A water heater is worth having a plumber install. It's tied into your water and your gas or electric, and a mistake there is the kind you find out about later.

sections.heading: Before You Call
body: If you can do it safely, check a few things first. Is the breaker on? Is the thermostat set where you want it? Is there water around the base of the tank?
If you smell gas, leave the house and call your gas company before anything else. If water is coming from the tank, turn off the cold water supply to the heater. Then call us.

items.q: Do I need a whole new water heater?
items.a: Not always. A thermostat, an element or a gas valve can be the whole problem. If the tank itself has failed, we'll tell you so, and we replace water heaters too.

items.q: Can you come on a weekend?
items.a: We work seven days a week and don't charge emergency rates. Call and tell us what the heater is doing.

items.a: All three. We do residential, commercial and rental plumbing.

sections.heading: What Happens Before Anything Gets Dug

image.alt: Basement floor drain beside a washer and utility sink

body: A sewer problem and a sewer replacement are not the same thing. A clog, a root in a joint or a bad connection can look just like a failed pipe from the basement.

So we start by finding out what's actually wrong with the line. If clearing it or a smaller repair will solve the problem, we'll say so. If the pipe has really failed, we'll say that too, and tell you what replacing it takes.

sections.heading: Signs Your Sewer Line Needs Attention
body: Every sign here can mean a clog, and every one can mean a failing line. The point is to find out which before you spend money.

items.title: Backups in the lowest drain
items.text: A basement floor drain or the lowest tub that backs up when a fixture upstairs runs is the classic sign.

items.title: Gurgling toilets and drains
items.text: Air pushed back through a fixture when water goes down another one points to trouble in the line.

items.title: Slow drains all over the house
items.text: One slow sink is usually a local clog. Every drain slow at once points to the main line.

items.title: Clogs that keep coming back
items.text: Cleared once and back in a few weeks. Tree roots grow into joints and cracks, and they don't stop on their own.

items.title: A sewer smell, or a wet patch in the yard
items.text: Outside the house, a damp or sunken spot along the line's path can mean a break underground.

sections.quote: My main sewer line in the basement got clogged up due to tree roots. … He gave me a flat price(very good price, compared to other businesses) and came out within an hour and got the drain unclogged even use the camera to show me what was going on inside the sewer line without any extra charge.

sections.heading: Clear, Repair or Replace?
body: Here's how to think about it. A blockage gets cleared. A single bad section or joint may be a repair. A line that's cracked, collapsed, sagging or failing in several places is a replacement.
Ask any company that quotes you a new line how they know the old one has failed. If the answer is a guess, get a second look. If they looked and can show you, that's a better conversation.
We can't tell you from here which one you have. What we can tell you is that nothing gets decided until somebody has looked.

sections.quote: I've hired plumb crazy for multiple sewer and water line replacements as well as routine household plumbing items. Brandon is prompt, courteous and gets the job done right. I highly recommend Plumb Crazy!
sections.name: Keaton B.

sections.heading: What Replacement Involves

image.alt: Damp ground in a yard where a buried line may be leaking

body: When replacement is the answer, the old line comes out and a new one goes in, and that means digging. A sewer line carries everything out of the house toward the city main, so it isn't a job for guessing.
Before the work starts, we'll tell you where the line runs, what has to be opened up and what that means for your yard.

sections.heading: The Price Question
body: We can't give you a number for a line we haven't looked at, and we won't print one here. Once we've seen the job, you'll have the price in front of you before you decide.
If you already have quotes, tell us what they said and what they found. We'd like to hear it.

sections.heading: If Sewage Is Backing Up Now
body: Stop running water and don't flush. Whatever you send down has nowhere to go. Then call us and tell us where it's backing up.
We work seven days a week and don't charge emergency rates, so a backup on a weekend is a normal call.

items.q: How do I know I need a new sewer line?
items.a: You may not. A clog, a root or a bad joint can look the same as a failed pipe. Finding the real problem comes first, and we'll tell you what we find.

items.q: Can't the clog just be cleared?
items.a: Sometimes, yes. We clear sewer lines too. If clearing will solve it, that's what we'll tell you.

items.q: Will replacement tear up my yard?
items.a: Replacing a buried line means digging. We'll tell you what has to be opened up before the work starts.

items.q: Do you replace water lines too?
items.a: Yes. We repair and replace the water service line between the city main and the house.

lead.heading: Why we led with the smaller fix first
lead.text: The scariest moment for a Wichita homeowner is being handed a big quote and told it has to be done, with no way to tell if that's true. Looking for the smaller fix first, and telling you both options, answers it. We checked the five top Wichita competitors, and none of the sites we could read states it. Please tell us if that isn't how you work.
